Business context · API

Validate business API map

How authenticated people and tenant systems use the API, what each path changes, and which external services sit behind it.

What the API lets the business do

The API supports a multitenant administration service: platform administrators establish client tenants and their configuration; tenant staff manage tenant-owned resources and review operational logs; tenant machine clients synchronize supported records and validate tenant/device context. These paths rely on role claims and tenant scoping rather than a single undifferentiated “authenticated” permission.

Most business paths are synchronous request/response operations. Tenant activation depends on SMTP delivery, while ATDP export crosses a queue and an external worker. The validation endpoints establish whether a tenant, branch, terminal and device context is valid; they do not establish the result of an external biometric identity check.

The route inventory is grounded in controller attributes and the backend’s API notes. The generated Swagger route is documented below, but its live schema was not read in this run.

Permission and authentication model

JWT bearer authentication is accepted from the access_token cookie or an Authorization bearer header. The Angular portal establishes an encrypted ECDH session before human login; successful human login sets access, refresh and CSRF cookies. Refresh rotates the refresh session. Tenant API clients use a separate client-credential login to obtain a bearer JWT.

Journey: Provision and activate a tenant

Business purpose: give a client organisation a persisted tenant configuration and an activated tenant-administrator account.

  1. A platform administrator calls POST /api/tenant. The API validates tenant identity, persists the active tenant and settings, and encrypts stored connection credentials.
  2. The administrator creates a tenant administrator through POST /api/tenants/{tenantId}/tenant-admins. The service stores an activation token and expiry and attempts to send an activation email.
  3. The recipient submits the token and a password to POST /api/auth/tenant-admin/activate. A valid token is consumed and the forced-password-change state is cleared.
  4. The tenant administrator signs in through POST /api/auth/login/tenant; subsequent tenant operations are constrained by the authenticated tenant context.

Branches: duplicate RNEC and invalid tenant data are rejected; failed initial email delivery does not undo account creation and can be recovered by resending activation; invalid or expired tokens must not activate the account. Runtime email delivery and the user-visible error copy were not exercised.

Entities: `business-data-context#flow-tenant-provisioning`, `#flow-account-activation`, `#state-tenant`, `#state-tenant-admin`. Features: `business-e2e-context#feature-tenant-lifecycle`, `#feature-auth-session`.

Journey: Synchronize and validate tenant context

Business purpose: allow a tenant system to maintain supported resource records and check whether a submitted branch, terminal and device context belongs to its authenticated tenant.

  1. The client obtains a bearer JWT from POST /api/auth/login/api.
  2. Authenticated synchronization calls under /api/synchronize read the tenant claim and create, update or query supported branch, terminal and application-user records.
  3. The client calls POST /api/validation/mac-serial or POST /api/validation/api-access. These actions explicitly require the TenantApi policy.
  4. The validation service checks tenant ownership and configured branch, terminal MAC and device serial, then returns a context-validation result.

Branches: invalid credentials, missing tenant claims, or unknown and cross-tenant resource identifiers must not produce a successful context result. Synchronization routes require a valid authenticated principal and use tenant-scoped helpers; their actions do not name the TenantApi policy, so the intended accepted principal set needs a focused authorization check.

Boundary: these APIs validate tenant/device context; the external biometric decision and any resulting NR log creation are outside this verified call chain.

Entities: `business-data-context#flow-tenant-api-validation`, `#state-tenant-api-token`, `#entity-resource-ownership`. Features: `business-e2e-context#feature-api-sync-validation`.

Journey: Review operational logs

Business purpose: let platform and tenant users inspect filtered operational records without changing authoritative tenant or device records.

  1. An authorized user requests consultation, request, or unsatisfactory-response records through the corresponding GET /api/logs/… route.
  2. System administrators use global routes; tenant administrators and application users use the mis-… routes, which derive tenant scope from the authenticated principal.
  3. The service queries the configured MongoDB log collection and returns filtered, paginated records for display.

Branches: an expired session or insufficient role is denied; invalid filter/date ranges, no matches, and MongoDB unavailability affect the result. The exact runtime error response and UI recovery state were not exercised. Log retention and sensitivity obligations remain unverified.

Entities: `business-data-context#entity-operational-logs`, `#flow-log-review`. Feature: `business-e2e-context#feature-logs`.

Journey: Request and retrieve an ATDP export

Business purpose: request an export for a tenant and date range, then retrieve a generated document when the external worker has it available.

  1. A system administrator submits POST /api/logs/atdp/export. The API validates the tenant RNEC and date range, then persists an AtdpDownload record as Pendiente.
  2. After the database write, the API publishes the request identifier and range to RabbitMQ. The endpoint returns the created request identifier.
  3. The queue consumer and status writer are external to the inspected backend. An administrator can inspect requests through GET /api/logs/atdp/downloads.
  4. For document retrieval, a system administrator calls GET /api/logs/atdp?clientId=…&nut=…; a tenant log user calls GET /api/logs/atdp/mine?nut=…, where the tenant is derived from the token.

Branches: a queue-publish failure can leave a persisted request pending without a compensating update. Worker timeout, connection, or response failures map to service-unavailable behavior; a missing NUT maps to not found. Completion and the writer for later status transitions were not verified.

Entities: `business-data-context#flow-atdp-export`, `#state-atdp-download`, `#entity-atdp-download`. Feature: `business-e2e-context#feature-atdp`.

Architecture behind the API

The Angular portal and tenant machine clients enter through nginx and reach the ASP.NET API. The API applies middleware for error handling, security headers, payload decryption, authentication, CSRF, single-use API tokens and authorization before controller actions. Application services coordinate persistence and external calls.

Discovery gaps

  • OpenAPI contract: no static OpenAPI JSON was found, and no api-schema MCP provider was available. The local Compose Swagger document was fetched on 2026-10-22, as recorded in .context/project-config.md, but was not re-fetched during this refresh. Controller attributes and backend API notes remain the approved route-inspection substitute; schema-to-wire correspondence and runtime status contracts were not revalidated here.
  • Machine login payload: the route accepts client ID and secret headers plus a request DTO, but the DTO’s wire encoding was not verified. The map does not assert plaintext or encrypted body shape.
  • Synchronization authorization: actions use generic [Authorize] and derive tenant scope from claims, while validation actions name the TenantApi policy. Confirm the intended accepted principals and cross-tenant rejection behavior with contract/runtime evidence.
  • ATDP completion: the queue consumer and writer for EnProceso, Finalizado, Fallido and SinResultado are outside the inspected backend. A pending row may remain after queue publication failure.
  • Runtime contracts: user-visible status/body mappings, activation email receipt, MongoDB outage handling, and tenant isolation for negative cases were not exercised against a running API.
  • External transaction: the API’s context validation does not expose the external biometric result or prove which component creates corresponding NR logs.
